'''Robert Bruce Meyer''' (October 13,  1943 [[St. Louis]]- November 17, 2023)<ref>biographical information from ''American Men and Women of Science'', Thomson Gale 2004</ref> was an American physicist and professor at [[Brandeis University]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Robert B. Meyer|website=Martin A. Fisher School of Physics, Brandeis University|url=https://www.brandeis.edu/departments/physics/people/faculty/meyer.html}}</ref>

Meyer graduated from [[Harvard University]] in 1965 with a bachelor's degree and in 1970 with a doctoral degree with advisor [[David Turnbull (materials scientist) | David Turnbull]]<ref name=CV/> and dissertation on effects of electromagnetic fields on the structure of [[liquid crystal]]s.<ref name=MRS>{{Cite web |url= https://www.mrs.org/docs/default-source/Careers/awards/turnbull/david-turnbull-autobiography.pdf?sfvrsn=28bad611_2|title= David Turnbull Autobiography|pages=45–46|work= Official website|publisher= Materials Research Society|date= |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221108164228/https://www.mrs.org/docs/default-source/Careers/awards/turnbull/david-turnbull-autobiography.pdf?sfvrsn=28bad611_2 |archive-date=8 November 2022}}</ref> At Harvard, Meyer was a postdoctoral student and became in 1971 an assistant [[professor]] and in 1974 an associate professor. At [[Brandeis University]] he was appointed an associate professor in 1978 and a full professor in 1985.<ref name=CV/>

He was a visiting professor in 1977 of [[Nordita]] at [[Chalmers University of Technology|Chalmers University]] in Gothenburg and in 1978 Joliot Curie Professor at the École Supérieure de Physique et de Chimie Industrielle in Paris.<ref name=CV/>

{{blockquote|His research has concerned various aspects of the physics and chemistry of liquid crystals, including fundamental studies of liquid crystal ordering in a variety of systems, electric and magnetic field effects, [[defect structure]]s, phase changes, and the relationship between molecular structure and novel macroscopic properties such as [[flexoelectricity]] and [[ferroelectricity]].  Recently, his research has concentrated on liquid crystalline gels and [[elastomer]]s, and textures and modulated phases in ferroelectric liquid crystals.<ref name=CV>{{cite web|title=Robert B. Meyer, CV and list of publications|url=https://www.brandeis.edu/departments/physics/people/faculty/CVs/meyer_vita_11.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110913135000/https://www.brandeis.edu/departments/physics/people/faculty/CVs/meyer_vita_11.pdf |archive-date=13 September 2011}}</ref>}}

In 2006 Meyer received, jointly with [[Noel A. Clark]], the [[Oliver E. Buckley Condensed Matter Prize]] for basic theoretical and experimental studies of liquid crystals, in particular their ferroelectric and chiral properties (laudation).<ref>[http://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?last_nm=Meyer&first_nm=Robert&year=2006 Buckley Prize 2006]</ref> He was elected in 1985 a Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]]<ref>{{cite web|website=American Physical Society|title=Fellows from Brandeis University|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=&year=&unit_id=&institution=Brandeis+University}}</ref> and received the 2004 Benjamin Franklin Medal of the Franklin Institute.
